title: 2  How science works
text:
2.1 How does science work?
How does science work? How do we think or claim that science works? How does it work ‘really’ or in practice?
The aim is, first, to help students to develop an understanding of how scientists or metascientists (those who study science) have described and explained how science works or should work: objective seeking after truth (Merton); the assumption and falsification testing of hypotheses (Popper), risky hypotheses (Meehl); the consolidation and the disruption of scientific paradigms (Kuhn); networks of power (Bourdieu, Greenhalgh); science as a messy business in practice (Chang).
In meeting this aim, we hope to enable students, second, to situate themselves appropriately as critically reflective citizen scientists within a scientific culture that is historically rooted and capable of change.
Given their participation in class activities, students should be able to identify different ways of “doing science”, and should be able to demonstrate an awareness of the conditions (including the inequities) or historical contingencies that may help to explain what scientists do.
We may consider, also, as relevant to questions about why scientists choose to do what they do:

text:
What we learn from the history and philosophy of science

title: 3  What is theory?
text:
3.1 What is a good theory and what makes a theory good?
As scientists, we often claim to build or to test theory: what is a theory, how can some theories work or be better than others?
If we are not building theory, what are we doing (or should we be doing)? How do we get from concerns or questions about people and their attributes or behaviours to scientific research and (some of) its products: theoretical accounts or scientific understanding?
Researchers have worked, or claimed to work, to improve research practices or processes (e.g., promulgating open science recommendations and building associated resources) but this focus on process has latterly revealed what some call the ‘theory crisis’. There is now an understanding that hypothesis testing may be premature in some areas of research (where primary description may be more useful), that theories may be more or less weakly specified or ambiguous, and that we (as researchers or consumers of research) should demand or seek to build better or more useful theories.
Our aim here is to enable students to identify, first, what theories look like, what features characterize good or better theories, and what theory-like objects look like, so that students can distinguish between theories and their distractors (e.g., acronyms, stories, metaphors or statistical summaries), and can identify theoretical accounts or their components, even when these accounts may not be explicitly communicated or identified as such in venues like journal articles.
In meeting this aim, we hope, second, to enable students to critically evaluate research presentations that purport to (and do or do not) present theoretical accounts or tests of theoretical accounts, to parse such accounts for their constituent assumptions, to identify their limitations or weaknesses.
Given their learning, students should be able to evaluate theories, propose modifications to theories, and develop research programmes aimed at probing or uncovering theoretical limitations or adjudicating between theoretical alternatives.

title: 4  Working with evidence
text:
4.1 Hypothesis testing, sampling, and power, precision, bias, and variation
Given our research aims, objectives, theories or questions, how do we test our beliefs against the evidence that, in the empirical psychological sciences, we might typically expect to acquire?
The dominant paradigm in psychological science comprises a procedure centered on what is known as Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST). This procedure is difficult to teach and understand and is mostly taught incorrectly or misunderstood (or so studies of NHST suggest). What does it involve? What are the common misunderstandings? What, actually, do we want to do when we want to test our beliefs against evidence, or to learn from our observations?
What is the value of evidence that derives from the samples we often see (in papers) or that we expect to collect in the psychological sciences? We consider theory or belief testing in the context of the practical realities of how scientific research is (imperfectly) realized by human researchers to more or less useful ends. What do we learn from recent crises about problematic or questionable research practices (to the extent they exist)? How do we identify a way to reason effectively about evidence or claims about evidence, by comparison?
Our aim is, first, to equip students to understand what researchers say they are doing when they claim to be testing hypotheses, to identify what we can or cannot conclude from reported tests (tests as reported or presented versus tests as practised), given samples of various kinds (varying in size or representativeness).
In meeting this aim, we hope, second, to enable students to critically evaluate the utility or quality of research findings, given reported tests and data samples. Concerns about the utility of NHST and the informativeness of samples of various kinds intersect, here, because limitations in sampling (e.g., the prevalence of small convenience samples in developmental research) combine with the inappropriate use of NHST, especially in the context of weak theories, to yield inconsistent, noisy, or uncertain estimates or tests.
Given their learning, students should be able to calibrate their response to findings reported in individual reports, or in groups of reports, given study sample-test combinations or given field normative sampling test practices.

title: 11  Setting up a book in Quarto
text:
11.1 Introduction
We want the production of the book to be self-documenting. This will allow us to share Quarto process information. Opening chapters begin with book level stuff. Later chapters focus on within-chapter content writing and editing.
This chapter gets you from nothing to the skeleton structure of a book, published as live webpages through GitHub Pages.

title: 11  Setting up a book in Quarto
text:
11.2 New project, GitHub first
We are going to take an approach set out here (there are others). It helps us to understand how to work where there is an existing GitHub repository.
https://happygitwithr.com/new-github-first

11.2.1 Make a repo on GitHub
Go to https://github.com and make sure you are logged in.
You will see your profile page.






Figure 11.1: GitHub new repo



Near ‘Repositories’, click the big green ‘New’ button. Or, if you are on your own profile page, click on ‘Repositories’, then click the big green ‘New’ button.


11.2.2 Name the repository, add a description, keep it public, add a README, add .gitignore, add a license






Figure 11.2: github-new-repo-name-public



You will have to enter some information:

Repository template: No template.
Repository name: myrepo or whatever you wish to name your new project. Approach this similar to a variable name, in code: descriptive but brief, no whitespace. Letters, digits, -, ., or _ are allowed.
Description: any short description of the project.
Public.
Initialize this repository with: Add a README file.
Click the big green button that says Create repository.







Figure 11.3: github-new-repo-name-public-values



Now click the big green button that says <> Code. Copy a clone URL to your clipboard. You will need this for the R-Studio side of the set-up.






Figure 11.4: github-new-repo-url





11.2.3 Now, in RStudio, set up a project (GitHub repo first)
We are going to create a project, using version control.
File > New Project > Version control






Figure 11.5: rstudio-create-project-version-control



We will be cloning a project from a Git repository: the repo we just created.
File > New Project > Version control > Git






Figure 11.6: rstudio-create-project-version-control-git



Enter the URL from the GitHub repository.

Remember where we got the URL:







Figure 11.7: github-new-repo-url



In RStudio, enter the URL in the Clone Git Repository dialogue box.






Figure 11.8: rstudio-create-project-version-control-git-url



Click on Create Project.
The project folder (and all its contents) is now on your local hard drive.






Figure 11.9: mac-finder-project





11.2.4 Check that our local drive and the remote repository are connected
Now, in RStudio, you can check that your local drive folder and the remote repository on GitHub are connected.

Open the README.md. Edit it. Save the edit.
Click on the Git tab (top right window). Notice that the README.md file is now associated with a blue M under Status.

In RStudio > Git

Click on the button box under Staged to get a tick in the box.
Click on the Commit button above.







Figure 11.10: rstudio-git-commi




A window opens.
Review the changes you have staged. Deletions are shown in red. Additions are shown in green.
Enter a brief but informative message in the commit message box. Click on Commit.







Figure 11.11: rstudio-git-commit-message




Best practice advice is to commit often, push less frequently.
RStudio > Git We click on Push to test the connection.

Assuming the connection is good, clicking on the Push will show you a window showing a summary of what has been changed in (pushed up to) the repo.






Figure 11.12: rstudio-git-commit-message-push



Now, in GitHub, you can check that your local drive folder and the remote repository on GitHub are connected.

At the repo webpage, you can see the commit message, a with a timestamp.
This is why it is wise to write informative messages: you want to know what you did when.
You can click on a file name to see the edits.







Figure 11.13: github-commits-edits



That was pushing. How about pulling?

Click on the Pull button.







Figure 11.14: rstudio-git-pulln




It works i.e. you can get changes to the repository downloaded to your local drive but there are no changes and everything is up to date.



11.2.5 Create a new book
Let’s say I don’t already have a book but I want to create a book, and I want to make a Quarto book. We can create a set of files to act as a skeleton for the book we are going to write.
In RStudio, in the terminal, we write the command:
quarto create project book .
The trailing dot tells Quarto to use the current directory rather than making a new subfolder.

You will be asked to enter a title.

In the terminal, you will see results that look like this. The directory information will be different.






Figure 11.15: rstudio-terminal-quarto-create-book



This bash code (a sequence of code entered at the terminal) creates _quarto.yml, index.qmd, intro.qmd, summary.qmd, references.qmd, and references.bib.

You can see these files have appeared in the folder you are working with.







Figure 11.16: rstudio-files-project-book-files





11.2.6 Working with the book yaml
In RStudio, in the script window, in the open _quarto.yml file, we can see some pre-populated information and the title we entered.






Figure 11.17: rstudio-script-yaml-defaults




Edit the yaml to substitute the prepopulated author name with your name.
Save.



11.2.7 Preview what we have got so far.
Click on Render in RStudio, or run quarto preview in the Terminal.
Your default browser will open a live preview that updates as you edit and save .qmd files.
Let’s say I run quarto preview in the terminal. This is what I see in the terminal.






Figure 11.18: rstudio-terminal-quarto-preview



A new webpage tab should open. Here is what Safari shows me:






Figure 11.19: safari-browser-quarto-preview



Notice that in RStudio > Terminal, you can see a red button and the message
Watching files for changes
Browse at http://localhost:5105/
Listening on http://127.0.0.1:5105/
GET: /

Click on the red button and the Preview stops.

This preview is local to you. In the next step, we publish what we have got so far so anyone can view it, if they have the URL.
There are two ways to do this:

The simplest: run quarto publish gh-pages from the Terminal. This renders the book, pushes it to an auto-created gh-pages branch, and GitHub Pages picks it up automatically.
Alternative: set ‘output-dir: docs’ in _quarto.yml, render, commit the docs/ folder, add a .nojekyll file, and point GitHub Pages at the docs/ folder in Settings > Pages.

I am going to use the second route.


11.2.8 Publish your new book to live webpages
In Rstudio, in the script window, in _quarto.yml, set the output directory.

Edit the yaml, adding on a new line: output-dir: docs.







Figure 11.20: rstudio-script-yaml-book-docs



In Rstudio, in the terminal, enter touch .nojekyll.
Add a .nojekyll file to your repo root (touch .nojekyll in Terminal, or copy NUL .nojekyll on Windows). This stops GitHub from running its own Jekyll processor over your site, which can break Quarto’s output.
In Rstudio, in the terminal, quarto render.

The terminal will display its progress through the rendering process.
A review of the contents of the folder will show the new /docs/ folder.

In Rstudio, in git, commit all the new files. Then push.






Figure 11.21: rstudio-git-commit-new-all



Commit all new book files.

11.2.8.1 Fix the license
We might not have already done this but we need to choose a license for our materials.
In GitHub, change the license to CC.0
Before doing anything else, I pull this remote change to the local version.






Figure 11.22: rstudio-git-pull-license-edit





11.2.8.2 Publish the book
Point GitHub Pages at /docs
On GitHub.com, go to your repo’s Settings > Pages. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch, Branch to main, and folder to /docs. Save.






Figure 11.23: github-pages-point-to-docs





11.2.8.3 Check the live site
GitHub will build and deploy within a minute or two. Your site will be live at https://.github.io//. Any time you edit content, re-run quarto render, commit the updated docs/ folder, and push — no separate publish command needed with this method.

You can see that the book has now deployed to a live webpage in the Deployments column of the GitHub view of your repository.







Figure 11.24: github-deployment




If you click on the button github-pages, you get taken to a deployment information window:







Figure 11.25: github-deployment-info




where you can see a link (shown as the URL) to the now live webpage:

https://robayedavies.github.io/teaching-methods-critical-thinking/
Let’s move next to write or to make edits to some content.

Mostly, we would expect to work to write or to make edits to content for a book like this book in the following workflow.
If you click on the files e.g. the references.bib file then you can see the file contents and a pencil at the top of the file view window. If you clicked on the pencil, you could edit the file contents directly through the GitHub web interface.

section: 12.2 The typical workflow: thinking about the sequence of actions
text:
12.2 The typical workflow: thinking about the sequence of actions
Typically, you may proceed as follows: we assume that we are working in RStudio, in the context of the .Rproj folder for the project.

I may sensibly begin in the Git window in RStudio (RStudio/Git) by clicking on Pull to check if any changes have been made to the project following my last action, and to pull down those changes from the remote repository to my local version of the repository.
I create a file or edit a file.
I save the changes.
I commit and push the changes from my local to the remote repository.
Maybe I’ll preview the results of the changes.
I cycle through these changes until I am ready to render.
I render.
I push the changed or new files resulting from the render process.

title: 12  Quarto workflow overview
text:
12.3 Creating or editing content
We can think about creating or editing content in terms of multiple aspects. We can distinguish these aspects though we may not always be working on all of them:

Structure – working with parts, chapters, sections, blocks, divs and spans;
Content – text, images, computation inline or in code chunks;
Cross-references – to other book parts, to chapters, and to sections, figures, tables, files and other resources, and links to external webpages.

Information on book structure is here:
https://quarto.org/docs/books/book-structure.html

https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html#sec-divs-and-spans

title: 13  Introduction working with Quarto
text:
13.1 Organizing a book into parts and chapters
I have a rough idea in mind for a draft structure of parts and chapters. The book will be split into two parts:
I’ll edit the yaml to add in the parts I’m thinking about right now.
---
title: "[quarto file name.qmd]"
editor: visual
---
intro.qmd -> introduction.qmd summary.qmd -> conclusions.qmd
The _quarto.yml now looks like this:
project:
  type: book
  output-dir: docs

book:
  title: "Teaching critical thinking"
  author: "Rob Davies"
  date: "9/15/2026"
  chapters:

    - index.qmd

    - part: "Critical thinking"

    - introduction.qmd

    - how-science-works.qmd
    - what-is-theory.qmd
    - evaluating-evidence.qmd
    - lying-cheating.qmd
    - criticality-in-writing.qmd
    - criticality-in-visualization.qmd
    - critical-citation-practice.qmd
    - subjectivity-objectivity-virtues.qmd

    - conclusions.qmd    
    
    - part: "Quarto"

    - set-up-book.qmd
    - workflow-overview.qmd    
    - markdown-basics.qmd

    - part: "References"

    - references.qmd

bibliography: references.bib

editor: visual

format:
  html:
    theme:
      - cosmo
      - brand
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrreprt
The process of rendering changes the contents of the folder. We see the creation of new .html files, corresponding to the new chapters. We see deletion of the html files corresponding to the .qmd files I renamed.

title: 13  Introduction working with Quarto
text:
Content for teaching and learning, focused on critical thinking;
Self-documenting writing and producing the book in Quarto.



I’ll also create a bunch of empty .qmd files with the titles of the chapters I’m thinking about. This is so that the index process associated with the yaml can work without error:
You create a new .qmd by going to: RStudio/File/New File/Quarto Document ... – and clicking on the Create Empty Document at the bottom of the dialogue box.
When you do this, each new empty file will be created with a minimal yaml section e.g.:



To reduce redundancy, I’m going to delete the editor: visual bit from each file. I will add it to _quarto.yml so that this property is then inherited by every book chapter .qmd.
I also need to rename the dummy files created when I first created the book. I can do this directly in the file folder.





And the RStudio window shows the new files in both the Files sub window or tab, and in the Git tab.
I commit the changes with the message: Set up book structure, edits to _quarto.yml and create empty .qmd files to hold content for new chapters.
I check the preview in terminal with quarto preview. Looks good.
I render the book with quarto render.








Figure 13.1: rstudio-edits-changes-git-files




I first stage the changes: in RStudio/Git under the Staged column, click on the check box at the top of the lift, press and hold SHIFT, then click on the check box at the bottom of the list, to stage all file entries.
I commit the changes.
I push the changes. From the moment I push the changes, if I go to the web view of my repository, I should be able to see that the deployment to GitHub Pages has been refreshed, and the resulting downstream web page should represent the revised book structure.
It does.







Figure 13.2: github-repo-pages-deployment-update




The output looks ok in Safari:







Figure 13.3: safari-webpage-book-structure-revised

title: 13  Introduction working with Quarto
section: 13.2 Writing content: adding text, adding sections, adding callout boxes, and inserting images
text:
13.2 Writing content: adding text, adding sections, adding callout boxes, and inserting images

13.2.1 Adding text
The basics of adding text is covered here:
https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html#links-images
And most of the time, we are writing stuff like this:

### Adding text

The basics of adding text is covered here: 

<https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html#links-images>



13.2.2 Adding sections
Most of the time, we are going to divide our text into sections or into callout boxes.
In Quarto, we use # marks to identify section headers, varying the number of # to indicate the level of section header.

# Heading 1

## Heading 2

### Heading 3

#### Heading 4

##### Heading 5

###### Heading 6

Quarto will automatically number the sections, and number the sections, unless we specify otherwise.
We can tell Quarto to do this explicitly in the book yaml or in a chapter yaml. We can edit the book yaml _quarto.yml to be explicit about the behaviour we want.

format:
  html:
    theme:
      - cosmo
      - brand
    number-sections: true  
  pdf:
    documentclass: scrreprt
    number-sections: true


13.2.2.1 Cross-referencing sections
Cross references are an important facet of writing Quarto documents. We can add code to enable automatic referencing of equations, figures, images, sections and tables.
https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#sections
Let’s say we have a section ### Inserting images, we can refer to the section as follows:

### Inserting images {#sec-inserting-images}

This means that we can then write the code:

@sec-inserting-images


to get this: Section 13.2.4.




13.2.3 Adding callout boxes
It is often helpful to use callout boxes. We probably ought to be systematic or consistent about this across chapters (and across the contributions of different authors).
You can find information about callout boxes here:
https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html#callouts
We often want to use one of the following variety of callout boxes – notice that we can label boxes for cross-referencing:

::: {#tip-example .callout-tip}
## Cross-Referencing a Tip

Add an ID starting with `#tip-` to reference a tip.
:::

See @tip-example...







Tip 13.1: Cross-Referencing a Tip



Add an ID starting with #tip- to reference a tip.


See Tip 13.1…

::: {#nte-example .callout-note}
## Cross-Referencing a note

Add an ID starting with `#nte-` to reference a note.
:::

See @nte-example...







Note 13.1: Cross-Referencing a note



Add an ID starting with #nte- to reference a note.


See Note 13.1…

::: {#wrn-example .callout-warning}
## Cross-Referencing a warning

Add an ID starting with `#wrn-` to reference a tip.
:::

See @wrn-example...







Warning 13.1: Cross-Referencing a warning



Add an ID starting with #wrn- to reference a tip.


See Warning 13.1…

::: {#imp-example .callout-important}
## Cross-Referencing a important

Add an ID starting with `#imp-` to reference something important.
:::

See @imp-example...







Important 13.1: Cross-Referencing a important



Add an ID starting with #imp- to reference something important.


See Important 13.1…

::: {#cau-example .callout-caution}
## Cross-Referencing a caution

Add an ID starting with `#cau-` to reference a caution.
:::

See @cau-example...







Caution 13.1: Cross-Referencing a caution



Add an ID starting with #cau- to reference a caution.


See Caution 13.1…
Most usefully, we can create boxes that are collapsible and that we can cross-reference:

::: {#nte-optional-command .callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional heading

Your content here — this could include a code chunk, plain text, or both.
:::

See @nte-optional-command for the optional command.







Note 13.2: Optional heading





Your content here — this could include a code chunk, plain text, or both.



See Note 13.2 for the optional command.


13.2.4 Inserting images
I am going to do this by example through editing the Quarto how-to files, to make this book building process self-documenting.
If you insert an image in a .qmd, you use syntax like this:

![Caption](elephant.png)


where [Caption] the text in square brackets is the caption text, and (elephant.png) the file name in round brackets identifies the image file.

https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html#links-images

13.2.4.1 Working with a set of multiple images so that you need to organize them in a folder and locate them in the Quarto image insertion syntax
I might have to work with multiple image files, so I will collect them in a single folder.
I am going to insert images showing screen shots of the workflow elements. I think it’ll be easier to do this, and tidier, if I locate all the image .png files in a single /files/ folder in the Quarto book working directory.
If I do this, then identifying the file requires me to use syntax to identify both the image and its location (file path):

![Caption](/files/elephant.png)


/files/ – tells Quarto that the .png is located in the files subfolder.
the /.../ use of forward slashes before and after the folder name tells Quarto that the folder is (with the first /... ) located at the top level of the book project folder (the project root).

Typically, we are going to use syntax like this with a folder structure like this:
my-book/
├── _quarto.yml
├── index.qmd
├── chapter1.qmd
├── chapter2/
│   └── chapter2.qmd
└── files/
    └── elephant.png

I create the new folder: files in the book project folder.
I copy the screen shot .png files into the /files/ folder.
I commit the change: “Create a new files folder, and copy in screen shot images.”
I push the changes though this may take a while.

Note that if I wanted to organize the files to a sub-folder (not project root) then provided that folder lives at the same level as the .qmd referencing the image file, I would use this syntax: ![Caption](files/elephant.png) – omitting the first forward slash.


13.2.4.2 Editing the image insertion syntax so that you have a caption, you set up figure referencing, you edit the sizing and you specify location
Most of the time, you are going to want to do five things when you include an image in a .qmd file. You will need to:

Identify the file, and identify its location to Quarto;
Add a caption;
Add a hidden figure label so that you can refer to the image later;
Specify the size of the output image;
Add alt text (for html output) to enable accessibility for people using screen readers.

We have seen that you use syntax like this:

![rstudio-edits-changes-git-files](/files/rstudio-edits-changes-git-files.png)


to ![...] add caption text;
to (/files/...) identify the location of the folder holding the image file, by naming the folder files, and specifying its location relative to the root (the top level) of the project folder /.../;
to ...(...rstudio-edits-changes-git-files.png) identify the file holding the image we want to present.

If we use the following code, we can specify further information:

![rstudio-edits-changes-git-files](/files/rstudio-edits-changes-git-files.png){#fig-rstudio-edits-changes-git-files width=60% fig-align="center" fig-alt="RStudio Git Window listing of file changes"}

In the {...} curly brackets, located immediately after the image file () we can specify:

fig-... a figure label;
width = ... image relative size information;
fig-align = ... alignment information;
fig-alt="..." alt text to enable accessible reading of our webpage.

Notice that different elements are separated by a single space inside {...}.
I can reference a figure using this cross-reference code:

@fig-rstudio-edits-changes-git-files

Provided Quarto can find the label fig-rstudio-edits-changes-git-files, using this code will let me say “I am referring to this Figure 13.1”. Here, Quarto replaces the code with an automatically numbered reference (and in html, live link to the image).

title: 14  Working with citations, references, and citation style guides
text:
14.1 Working with citations
You will be working with reference information.
Th Quarto guide to working with citations is here:
https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html
As it says there:
Quarto will use Pandoc to automatically generate citations and a bibliography in a number of styles. To use this capability, you will need:
We will need to build a references list as we develop our writing, and we will want the citations in text and the reference list or lists that are produced to be presented following APA 7 style guidance.
crumbs: 14  Working with citations, references, and citation style guides

title: 14  Working with citations, references, and citation style guides
text:
A quarto document formatted with citations (see Citation Markdown).
A bibliographic data source, for example a BibLaTeX (.bib) or BibTeX (.bibtex) file.
Optionally, a CSL file which specifies the formatting to use when generating the citations and bibliography (when not using natbib or biblatex to generate the bibliography).



14.1.1 You will need a reference manager: Zotero is good.
I assume that you can work with a reference manager like Zotero:
https://www.zotero.org

14.1.1.1 Install and open Zotero
Have Zotero open and running on your machine while you write.
RStudio’s Visual Editor auto-detects a local Zotero installation and reads your library directly: no separate setup or API key needed for basic use.


14.1.1.2 Switch to Visual Editor mode
In RStudio, open your .qmd file and click the ‘Visual’ tab (top-left of the source pane, next to ‘Source’).
This switches from raw markdown editing to a WYSIWYG-style view that supports the citation picker.
You can switch back to Source mode any time — the underlying markdown is identical either way e.g.

@knuth84


If you write this key, then you get: Knuth (1984) – where you do the citation.



14.1.1.3 Insert a citation
With cursor where you want a citation, go to Insert > Citation (or the keyboard shortcut Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+F8).
Choose ‘Your Zotero Library’ as the source, search for the reference, and select it.


14.1.1.4 Quarto auto-adds it to references.bib
When you insert a Zotero citation this way, Quarto automatically adds the full reference entry to your references.bib file and inserts the citation key at your cursor — you don’t need to manually export or copy anything.


14.1.1.5 (Optional) Install Better BibTeX for stable citation keys
By default Zotero generates citation keys like davies2026 automatically. If you want more control over key format (e.g. author-year-word style, or matching a specific journal convention), install the Better BibTeX plugin for Zotero, then in RStudio go to Tools > Global Options > R Markdown > Citations and enable ‘Use Better BibTeX for citation keys’. ### Using a required style
We will need to present citations and the reference list using APA 7 style.


14.1.1.6 Download the APA CSL file
Go to https://www.zotero.org/styles and search ‘APA’.
Click on ‘American Psychological Association 7th edition’.
On the style’s page, right-click the download/link icon and choose ‘Save Link As’ to download the raw .csl file rather than letting your browser install it into Zotero.


14.1.1.7 Save it into your book’s project folder
Rename the downloaded file to something like apa.csl if it isn’t already, and place it in your project root — the same folder as _quarto.yml, alongside references.bib.
I am using psychological-bulletin.csl for now.


14.1.1.8 Point _quarto.yml at the CSL file
We edit the book yaml to add information on the .bib, the .csl, and how we want the citations to behave (in-text citations to hyperlink down to their entry in the reference list).

bibliography: references.bib
csl: psychological-bulletin.csl
link-citations: true



14.1.1.9 Render and check citations
Render or refresh your preview.
Your in-text citations and bibliography will now follow APA formatting — e.g. (Davies, 2026) in-text, and a properly formatted APA reference list where your #refs div sits, instead of Pandoc’s default numbered/bracketed style.




Knuth, D. E. (1984). Literate programming. Comput. J., 27(2), 97–111. https://doi.org/10.1093/comjnl/27.2.97
